_record_registry_protocols_observation
Function-registry surface required by the simulator/functions consumers.
    Each method maps directly to a ``registry.<method>`` callsite. Keep this
    protocol synchronised with the actual call surface; missing methods now
    raise ``AttributeError`` at the callsite rather than being silently routed
    through a duck-typed fallback.
RegistryProtocol.create_instance
RegistryProtocol.get_function_version
Single-parameter surface required by ``GraphValidator._validate_arity``.
    The canonical implementation is the ``StaticParam`` dataclass at
    ``openforage/functions/registry_and_store/_registry.py`` (frozen dataclass with field defaults
    ``default=None``, ``min=None``, ``max=None``, ``variadic=False``). The
    fields are present on every instance, so call sites read them directly
    rather than via ``hasattr``.
    Note: this Protocol describes the *parameter object* exposed via a
    registry entry's ``param_schema``. It is independent from the registry
    object itself (``RegistryProtocol``).
Typed registry and parameter protocols for simulator_engine consumers.
Active consumers:
- ``src.simulator_engine.evaluators.live_evaluation.LiveEvaluator`` (Round 8 β baseline).
- ``src.simulator_engine.evaluators.expression_evaluator`` fast-path checks
  (``_can_use_simple_rank_fast_path``, ``_registry_allows_stub_fast_path``,
  ``_registry_can_instantiate``).
- ``src.simulator_engine.graph._combine._registry_has``.
- ``openforage.functions.evaluation_harnesses.similarity_analysis._has_state``.
- ``src.simulator_engine.graph.graph_validator._validate_arity`` reads
  ``ParamProtocol`` items from a registry entry's ``param_schema``.
- ``openforage.catalog.function_store.FunctionStore`` (SDK registry projection).
- ``openforage.runtime.core._build_function_registry`` (SDK bootstrap
  conformance/startup consumer).
Adding a new callsite on a method not declared here MUST come with a matching
extension of this protocol so that every registry implementation (production
and test) is forced to implement the new surface or fail loudly with
``AttributeError``. That fail-loud behaviour is the canonical bug surface and
replaces the prior duck-typed ``hasattr(registry, ...)`` fallback pattern.
- ``has_factory(name)`` feature-detects test-injected factories. Production
  ``ManifestFunctionStore``, ``EvaluationRegistry``, etc.) return ``False``
  unconditionally because none of them carry a ``_factories`` mapping. Test
  mocks that override behaviour by assigning ``mock._factories[name] = X``
  return ``name in self._factories`` so the existing fast-path bypass
  semantics are preserved.
- ``create_plugin`` is intentionally **not** declared on this protocol.
  ``similarity_analysis.pyx`` calls ``registry.create_plugin(name)`` inside a
  ``try/except`` that already falls back to ``create_instance``. Adding it
  here would force every registry — including those without aggregation
  plugin support — to declare the method, expanding the change surface
  without correctness benefit.

Decompress *data*, returning uncompressed data as bytes.
If *max_length* is nonnegative, returns at most *max_length* bytes of
decompressed data. If this limit is reached and further output can be
produced, *self.needs_input* will be set to ``False``. In this case, the next
call to *decompress()* may provide *data* as b'' to obtain more of the output.
If all of the input data was decompressed and returned (either because this
was less than *max_length* bytes, or because *max_length* was negative),
*self.needs_input* will be set to True.

*** A special note about internal error number 1007 ***
Experience suggests that a common cause of i.e. 1007
is unreliable memory or other hardware.  The 1007 assertion
just happens to cross-check the results of huge numbers of
memory reads/writes, and so acts (unintendedly) as a stress
test of your memory system.
I suggest the following: try compressing the file again,
possibly monitoring progress in detail with the -vv flag.
* If the error cannot be reproduced, and/or happens at different
  points in compression, you may have a flaky memory system.
  Try a memory-test program.  I have used Memtest86
  (www.memtest86.com).  At the time of writing it is free (GPLd).
  Memtest86 tests memory much more thorougly than your BIOSs
  power-on test, and may find failures that the BIOS doesn't.
* If the error can be repeatably reproduced, this is a bug in
  bzip2, and I would very much like to hear about it.  Please
  let me know, and, ideally, save a copy of the file causing the
  problem -- without which I will be unable to investigate it.

parent(x)
Return the parent of the element ``x``.
Usually, this means the mathematical object of which ``x`` is an
element.
- ``x`` -- an element
- If ``x`` is a Sage :class:`Element`, return ``x.parent()``.
- Otherwise, return ``type(x)``.
    `Parents, Conversion and Coercion <http://passagemath.org/docs/latest/html/en/tutorial/tour_coercion.html>`_
    Section in the Sage Tutorial
    sage: a = 42
    sage: parent(a)
    Integer Ring
    sage: b = 42/1
    sage: parent(b)
    Rational Field
    sage: c = 42.0
    sage: parent(c)                                                                 # needs sage.rings.real_mpfr
    Real Field with 53 bits of precision
Some more complicated examples::
    sage: x = Partition([3,2,1,1,1])
    sage: parent(x)
    sage: v = vector(RDF, [1,2,3])                                                  # needs sage.modules
    sage: parent(v)                                                                 # needs sage.modules
    Vector space of dimension 3 over Real Double Field
The following are not considered to be elements, so the type is
    sage: d = int(42)  # Python int
    sage: parent(d)
    sage: L = list(range(10))
    sage: parent(L)
    <... 'list'>

have_same_parent(left, right) -> bool
Return ``True`` if and only if ``left`` and ``right`` have the
same parent.
.. WARNING::
    This function assumes that at least one of the arguments is a
    Sage :class:`Element`. When in doubt, use the slower
    ``parent(left) is parent(right)`` instead.
    sage: from sage.structure.element import have_same_parent
    sage: have_same_parent(1, 3)
    sage: have_same_parent(1, 1/2)
    sage: have_same_parent(gap(1), gap(1/2))                                        # needs sage.libs.gap
These have different types but the same parent::
    sage: # needs sage.rings.real_mpfr
    sage: a = RLF(2)
    sage: b = exp(a)
    sage: type(a)
    <... 'sage.rings.real_lazy.LazyWrapper'>
    sage: type(b)
    <... 'sage.rings.real_lazy.LazyNamedUnop'>
    sage: have_same_parent(a, b)

Welcome to FabFilter $plugin! This help hint window gives you hints and tips when you move the mouse cursor over a control. It pops up after one second.
If you want to learn more, open the user manual by clicking Help Topics on the Help menu.
Tip: You can disable help hints by unchecking Show Interactive Help Hints on the Help menu.
The Undo button undoes the last change you made to the plug-in, for example when adjusting a knob or loading a preset.
The Redo button cancels the last undo command.
The A/B button switches between two plug-in states: A and B. Using this, you can quickly compare between two different states of the plug-in without having to save a preset.
The Copy button works together with the A/B button. It saves the current plug-in settings to both the A and B states. This enables you to switch back to the saved state later using the A/B button.
The Previous Preset button selects the previous preset in the presets menu.
The Presets button opens the presets menu, where you can open and save presets. For more information, see Presets in the help file.
The Next Preset button selects the next preset in the presets menu.
The Help button provides access to the help file, the FabFilter web site and the About dialog which shows plug-in version and license information.
Click the Full Screen button to enter full-screen mode, so $plugin will fill the entire screen. This allows you to make very precise changes.
You can leave full-screen mode by simply pressing the Escape key or clicking the Full Screen button again.
The MIDI Learn button enables or disables MIDI Learning. With MIDI learn, you can associate MIDI controller numbers with any parameter. When the button is activated, the interface will go into MIDI Learn mode, and the current controller number association are shown for all controls. Now, you can do the following to associate a controller number with a parameter:
1) Click any knob, slider or select button that is highlighted in the dimmed interface. You will see the current associated controller number or a '-' when it is not associated yet.
2) Adjust the slider or knob on your MIDI keyboard or MIDI controller that you want to associate with that parameter.
That is all! The parameter will now be controlled by the MIDI controller. To exit MIDI Learn mode, just click the MIDI Learn button again.
The MIDI Learn menu lets you control the current parameter associations. It contains commands to enable or disable MIDI globally, view all MIDI-parameter associations, clear specific associations or the entire mapping, save the mapping, or revert to the previous mapping.
The Resize / Scaling button selects between different interface sizes, ranging from small to large sizes, and sets the preferred interface scaling. Once you've chosen a setting, new instances of the plug-in will always open with the selected size and scaling.
If an option is greyed out, this means that the current display is too small to support this interface size.
Note that the VST3 format supports custom resizing: you can simply drag the edges of the plug-in window to resize to any size if your host supports this.
The Resize / Scaling button sets the preferred interface scaling. Once you've chosen a setting, new instances of the plug-in will always open with the selected scaling.
If an option is greyed out, this means that the current display is too small to support this scaling.
The instance menu button opens the preset browser where you can select presets, but also copy/paste instance settings, or pin instances with similar colors if they exist.
The bypass button toggles the instance between fully bypassed and normal state using soft bypassing. When bypassed, the instance interface is dimmed and the bypass button glows red to indicate that it is active.
The output button opens a panel with output settings, including the Emphasize button that helps you to identify the track you are working on.
By clicking and holding the Emphasize button at the top of the Output controls, you can temporarily raise the level of an instance by 6 dB; it can help you identify which tracks you are working on in a complex mix with many instances.

The Threshold knob sets the level of incoming audio data (via the side chain) below which the gain should be reduced.
Typically you adjust the threshold to match the character and level of the incoming audio signal, depending on the desired gating or expansion behavior.
Note: If the Upward style is selected, this knob controls the separate upward threshold parameter, which has a smaller range. Be careful with low threshold settings in combination with a high ratio in this case.
If set to less than 100 dB, the Range knob limits the amount of expansion or gating that Pro-G applies. You can use this for example to limit the amount of background noise reduction, or to expand only a specific area of the dynamic range.
The Ratio knob sets the proportional expansion amount for signals below the threshold. For example, a ratio of 5:1 means that for every dB under the threshold, a gain reduction of 5 dB will be applied. If the ratio is set to the maximum value (100), Pro-G works as a gate instead of an expander.
Note: If the Upward style is selected, this knob controls the separate upward ratio parameter, which has a smaller range. Be careful with high ratio settings in combination with a low threshold in this case.
The Attack knob sets the speed at which the gate/expander opens to let the sound through.
Note: Pro-G is highly program-dependent, so the actual attack time may be shorter or longer depending on the character of the incoming audio.
With the Style drop down menu, you can select one of the six available expander styles. Each style uses its own unique algorithm to realize a distinct sound and character. 
The first four styles work in the same way, applying regular downwards expansion. The Upward style switches to upwards expansion, which works and sounds quite different and uses Threshold and Ratio settings that are separate from the other styles. Finally, there's also a dedicated Ducking style.
See also 'Time controls, style and knee' in the help file.
The Hold knob specifies how much time the gate/expander is forced to stay open after it has been triggered.
Tip: Longer hold times help to avoid 'chattering' effects (the sound of the gate opening and closing repeatedly).
The Release knob sets the time that the gate/expander takes to recover after opening. The various expansion styles of Pro-G use different attack and release models, with different ways and varying degrees of program dependency.
The Lookahead knob sets how much time in advance Pro-G will use to anticipate peaks in the audio signal. Compensating a longer attack time with a bit of look-ahead can help to preserve punch and transients.
Note: You need to enable look-ahead separately with the Lookahead Enabled button next to this knob.
The Knee knob sets the 'roundness' of the expansion around the threshold, which can vary between 0 dB (hard knee) and 30 dB (soft knee). A soft knee can help the gate to open and close in a more natural, gradual way.
The level meter shows the output (bright blue) of the expander versus the input (dimmed blue). This way, you get a good insight in the gating or expansion that is being applied. 
If the meter has clipped, click on the clipping area to reset the clipping indication.
The Lookahead Enabled button lets you choose whether you want to use look-ahead or not. If you disable look-ahead and oversampling is turned off, the plug-in runs with zero latency.
The Expert button switches between normal mode and expert mode. In expert mode, the interface will resize to make advanced side chain controls available, together with separate Dry and Wet mix knobs.
The Show Display button provides a way to turn the moving level display on and off, in case you find it distracting while listening.
The Side Chain Input switch selects the input to be used as detection signal for the expander. By default, the normal input signal is used. If your host supports side chaining, you will be able to route a signal from another channel to the side chain inputs of Pro-G. Choose Ext to use the external signal as the side chain input for the expander.
See also 'External side chaining' in the help file.
The Side Chain level and mix knobs adjust the gain of the side chain input for the two expander channels independently. In L/R mode, the expander channels are connected to the left and right output channels; in M/S mode, they correspond to the mid and side components of the output signal.
For example, in L/R mode, the left inner knob controls the gain of the signal for the left expander channel. The outer ring controls where this signal is coming from: the left or right side chain input or a mix of both.
By default, in the stereo version of Pro-G, both channels are fed with the same, equally mixed signal. This means that both channels are 'stereo linked'.
In mono mode, only one input level knob is available to adjust the side chain input level.
With the Audition button, you can listen to the detection signal that is used by the expander. In M/S mode, you will hear the Mid signal on the left, and the Side signal on the right if audition is enabled.
Using the filter controller, you can filter the side chain input signal using a combined 48 dB/octave high-pass and low-pass filter, so the expander only triggers on a certain area in the frequency spectrum.
Use the Audition button below the filter controller to hear the result.
The combined Dry knob adjusts the level and panning of the dry (unprocessed) signal. The pan ring either controls left and right, or mid and side, depending on the channel mode (L/R or M/S).
The combined Wet knob adjusts the level and panning of the processed signal. The pan ring either controls left and right, or mid and side, depending on the channel mode (L/R or M/S).
The Channel Mode button selects L/R (Left/Right) processing or M/S (Mid/Side) processing. By default, Pro-G works in L/R mode.
In M/S mode, the stereo input signal will be converted to a Mid/Side signal. One internal expander channel will process the mid signal (the mono component of the audio), and the other internal channel will process the side signal (the stereo component of the audio signal). This enables you to expand the mid and side signals independently.
See 'Mid/Side processing' in the help file for more information.
The Oversampling button determines how many times the internal process is oversampled. You can consider to use oversampling when using a high ratio in combination with short attack or release times.
Generally, oversampling reduces aliasing at the cost of additional CPU usage. Note that Pro-G always introduces some latency when oversampling is on (see also the Lookahead Enabled button).
The Input level/pan knobs adjusts the gain and panning of the input signal, before it is routed to the expander signal and side chain inputs. The pan ring either controls left and right, or mid and side, depending on the channel mode (L/R or M/S).
With the input and output level buttons, you get access to the level/pan knobs to control the input and output level and panning of the expander. Click once to make the knobs appear or disappear again.
You can also click and drag directly on each button to adjust the input or output level right away. As with knobs, Alt-click the button to reset the level, and double-click to type a new value.
The Global Bypass button toggles the whole plug-in between fully bypassed and normal state. While the plug-in is bypassed, the display dims and a red light glows in the bypass button itself.
The Output level/pan knobs adjusts the gain and panning of the output signal, after it has been processed by the expander, and after the Dry and Wet mix knobs in the Expert section have been applied.
The pan ring either controls left and right, or mid and side, depending on the channel mode (L/R or M/S).
